They sell to the strategy too cheaply after good rival news and buy from it too dearly after bad rival news, until the peer's own release or analyst revisions make the transfer obvious.","why":"One firm's earnings release carries news about its peers: industry demand, input costs, pricing, the business cycle (Foster 1981, intra-industry information transfer). Ramnath (2002) finds that investors and analysts of firms that have not reported yet do not fully use the first announcers' news, so the non-announcers' returns can be predicted in the days after the announcement. The rival's release is a sharp, dated news event in the related stock, which itself has no filing that day. Limited attention (Hou 2007, Cohen and Frazzini 2008) predicts that the related stock prices that news slowly: investors in stock i watch i's own news flow, not each rival's release. The claim: after a large release-session reaction of announcer j (real 8-K Item 2.02 dates), j's most return-correlated peers that have not reported yet this season keep moving in the direction of j's reaction over the next sessions. The announcer itself is not traded, so this is not the announcer's own drift (H-0028/H-0033).","why_not_arbitraged":"The signal per peer is a fraction of the announcer's move and is noisy. The transfer can go either way (common industry news vs competitive gain), and it is spread over many small positions during crowded earnings seasons, so it uses up attention and capital in exactly those weeks. Thomas and Zhang (2008) even find overreaction that is corrected at the late announcer's own release weeks later, so the short-horizon sign is disputed in the literature and not obviously crowded. In the most liquid names it may well be arbitraged already; this card tests whether it is."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"After the close of session t, stock i (a LIQ-500 member that is not reporting itself, has had no 8-K Item 2.02 reaction session in the last 40 sessions, and is covered by the 8-K data) is among the peers_k most return-correlated peers of at least one member j whose release-session market-adjusted reaction on t is at least z_threshold standard deviations. side = sign of the sum of sign(reaction) over such announcers (+1: the announcers' news was good, i should outperform; -1: bad, i should underperform). No event where the sum is zero. Announcers themselves are never marked, so they stay among the unmarked peers.","horizons":[1,3,5,10,21],"primary_horizon_days":5},"notes":"Brief fit: US single stocks, LIQ-500 cross-section, 5-session hold, daily decisions, mechanism test declared. Family: reuses peer-lead-lag-diffusion (H-0013) because the economic claim is the same - news about one firm reaches related firms late - so the trials count together. Why this is not H-0013 again: H-0013 traded any weekly move of statistical peers (mostly noise and flows) and found nothing; this card fires only on a dated, verified information event (a large reaction on a real 8-K earnings release) and only in peers that have not reported yet, which is the setting where the accounting literature reports the transfer (Ramnath 2002). The peer map is still statistical (correlation of market-adjusted returns; no industry codes are loadable), which is the main dilution risk. It is also not the PEAD family: the announcer is never traded, and its own drift (K-0046) is not the object. If the test passes it adds a new, much larger event set built on the one event type that has repeatedly passed the lab's placebo test. Expected size, stated before the run (K-0053, K-0064): a z >= 3 release reaction in LIQ-500 is roughly a 5-10 % move; same-day peer co-movement in the literature is a small fraction of it, so the remaining 5-session drift per peer event is plausibly 10-30 bps. The LIQ-500 round trip is roughly 10-12 bps, so the mechanism can clear cost only at the upper half of that range, and the market-neutral strategy needs about 20 bps or more per event to reach Sharpe 0.5 over T-bills (1 % slots, about 2,000-3,000 events per year, invested mostly in earnings seasons). Most likely death: diffusion in the most liquid names is complete within the release session (K-0072), so the gross after the next open is below cost; second most likely: the strategy bar even if the mechanism passes, as with the announcer drift itself. Feasibility: events exist only from 2004-08 (8-K data); I expect several hundred announcers with |z| >= 3 per year and a few thousand peer events per year on several hundred distinct dates, far above the G1 minimums, concentrated in the four earnings seasons; the first third of dev starts around 2004-09. The 40-session 'not reported yet' filter halves the events in peak weeks. Coverage gaps of the 8-K data (K-0035) mean some peers that did report are not excluded; that dilutes but does not bias the sign. Diagnostics the Builder should report if it can (K-0036): events and dates per year, share of long vs short events, and the by-side abnormal return.","references":[{"cite":"Foster (1981) Intra-industry information transfers associated with earnings releases, Journal of Accounting and Economics","year":1981},{"cite":"Ramnath (2002) Investor and analyst reactions to earnings announcements of related firms: an empirical analysis, Journal of Accounting Research","year":2002},{"cite":"Hou (2007) Industry information diffusion and the lead-lag effect in stock returns, Review of Financial Studies","year":2007},{"cite":"Cohen, Frazzini (2008) Economic links and predictable returns, Journal of Finance","year":2008},{"cite":"Thomas, Zhang (2008) Overreaction to intra-industry information transfers?, Journal of Accounting Research (opposite-sign evidence at the late announcer's own release)","year":2008}],"signal":{"description":"Decisions after the close of each session t using data up to that close; trades at the open of t+1. (1) Returns: daily close-to-close total return r = (1+ret_co)*(1+ret_oc)-1. Market-adjusted return a_i,t = r_i,t minus the equal-weighted mean r of all universe members with a return on t. (2) Peer map, recomputed after the close of the last session of each month and used for the whole next month: for every universe member j, its peers_k peers are the other members with the highest Pearson correlation of a over the 252 sessions ending that day (both stocks need at least 200 common valid observations; fewer than peers_k qualifying stocks -> take those that qualify). (3) Announcers at t: members j with ea_reaction_day[t, j] == 1 and |z_j,t| >= z_threshold, where z_j,t = a_j,t / sd(a_j over the 63 sessions ending t-1), at least 40 valid observations, otherwise j is skipped. (4) Peer events at t: for every member i that is not itself an announcer at t, that has no ea_reaction_day == 1 in the 40 sessions ending t (it has not reported yet this season) and whose ea_reaction_day is not NaN on t (covered by the 8-K data), compute S_i,t = sum over announcers j at t with i in peers(j) of sign(z_j,t). An event fires if S_i,t != 0, with side = sign(S_i,t). (5) Book: each event opens a position in i with sign = side at the open of t+1, held for hold_days sessions (exit at the open of t+1+hold_days). A new event in the same stock replaces the old one (new side, new clock). The position is also closed at the next open after i's own ea_reaction_day == 1 (its own news ends the transfer claim), and at the first decision after i leaves the universe or stops trading. Weights: every open position has weight side * 0.01 of equity; if more than 100 positions are open, all are scaled to side / N_open so that gross <= 1. No hedge basket, no leverage; the net exposure is whatever the long and short events add up to. title: Earnings-release volume visibility premium - LIQ-500 dollar-neutral, long announcers with abnormally high release-session volume, short abnormally low, matched on reaction sign and size, hold 5 days

(late-arriving attention buyers pay up), and holders of quiet announcers who are not replaced by new buyers. In the short leg, the counterparty is the attention premium of the quiet announcer that fails to materialize.","why":"Investor-recognition / visibility (Merton 1987; Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin 2001): a stock that trades unusually heavily becomes visible to more investors, the investor base widens and demand rises over the following days and weeks, so price rises. At an earnings release every announcer gets some attention, but how much the release-session volume exceeds the stock's own normal volume measures how much NEW attention (and opinion divergence, Garfinkel and Sokobin 2006) the release created. Holding the size and the sign of the price reaction fixed, an announcer whose release drew abnormally high volume should outperform an announcer whose release drew abnormally little, independently of the direction of the news. Lerman, Livnat and Mendenhall report that this volume effect is incremental to earnings-surprise drift. The claim tested here is the one the lab left open after H-0014 (a volume effect needs volume tied to an identified event): real 8-K release sessions, a volume measure relative to the stock's own history, and both sides compared inside the same reaction-sign and reaction-size bin, so earnings drift (PEAD) cancels to first order.","why_not_arbitraged":"The premium per event is small (tens of basis points over a week) next to the idiosyncratic risk of a stock that just reported, so only a diversified, high-turnover book can collect it and spread costs eat a large share; the release-session volume is an ambiguous signal (it also accompanies bad news and disagreement), and the effect has to be harvested from both a long and a short leg across thousands of small, clustered positions during earnings seasons, which ties up capacity for a modest Sharpe."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"Session t is a real 8-K Item 2.02 reaction session of LIQ-500 member j (no candidate for j in the previous 5 sessions), and j's release-session abnormal dollar volume (log of day-t dollar volume over its 63-session mean from t-68 to t-6) is in the top 30 % (side +1) or bottom 30 % (side -1) of the abnormal volumes of the past 252 sessions' release candidates that fall into the same bin of reaction sign and reaction-size tercile (market-adjusted day-t return divided by its own 63-session volatility).","horizons":[1,3,5,10,21],"primary_horizon_days":5},"notes":"Brief fit: US single stocks, cross-sectional, 5-session hold, mechanism test declared. Why this family and not a new one: it is the visibility mechanism of H-0014 (high-volume-visibility-premium), so its trials count there. Why it is not a re-run of H-0014: H-0014 sorted ALL LIQ-500 stocks weekly on abnormal volume with no event and found nothing; its lesson's open question was that a volume effect 'needs volume tied to an identified event'. Here the event is a real 8-K release session (no date prediction, so the hit-rate problem of H-0023/H-0026/H-0032 does not arise), only announcers are compared, and only with announcers of the same reaction sign and size tercile. Why it is not post-earnings-announcement-drift again: the side does not follow the sign of the reaction (long and short legs both contain good and bad news in equal bins), so PEAD continuation cancels to first order; the PEAD stop rule (H-0031) is about following the reaction sign, which this card does not do. Both sides are marked, so the placebo mean should sit near zero (K-0025), and the sort is on volume relative to the stock's own history, so the marked and unmarked sets should not differ much in beta (K-0074). Expected size (K-0053, K-0064): the literature finds the premium strongest in smaller firms; for LIQ-500 I expect roughly 15-35 bps gross per event over 5 sessions against a round trip of about 6-12 bps (cost tiers 3/6 bps half-spread by liquidity rank). With about 1,000 marked events a year (8-K coverage is incomplete, K-0035) and 1/30 slots, a 25 bps gross effect gives roughly 5 %/y net on about 6 %/y volatility (Sharpe near 0.8); a 15 bps effect gives a Sharpe near 0.3, which fails the T-bill bar. So the most likely deaths are the cost ratio or the strategy bar, or the latest-third decay that K-0060 predicts. Timing: all inputs are known at the close of the reaction session (the 8-K flag is set on the first session whose close is at or after the EDGAR acceptance time); entry at the next open. Publication check: GKM (2001) falls before the first 8-K event (2005), so there is no pre-publication window for it; Garfinkel-Sokobin (2006) leaves only about a year before publication, so the publication-decay ratio will be noisy. Events start about 2005-08 (252-session pool after the 8-K start). The hedge basket of the 50 most liquid members is banded at 5 % of equity to avoid the daily re-equalising turnover suspected in H-0019 and H-0031.","references":[{"cite":"Gervais, Kaniel, Mingelgrin (2001) The high-volume return premium, Journal of Finance 56(3)","year":2001},{"cite":"Garfinkel, Sokobin (2006) Volume, opinion divergence, and returns: a study of post-earnings announcement drift, Journal of Accounting Research 44(1)","year":2006},{"cite":"Lerman, Livnat, Mendenhall, The high-volume return premium and post-earnings announcement drift (working paper, SSRN 1122463)"},{"cite":"Merton (1987) A simple model of capital market equilibrium with incomplete information, Journal of Finance 42(3)","year":1987}],"signal":{"description":"Inputs per stock j and session t: total return r = (1+ret_co)(1+ret_oc)-1, dollar_volume, tradable, and ea_reaction_day (sec_8k_item202). Decisions after the close of session t using data up to that close; trades at the open of t+1. (1) Event candidates: ea_reaction_day[t,j] == 1, j is a LIQ-500 member and tradable at t, and j had no candidate in the previous hold_days sessions (a second Item 2.02 filing within the hold is ignored). NaN ea_reaction_day = no event. (2) Reaction size: e = r[t,j] minus the equal-weight mean r of all LIQ-500 members at t; sigma = standard deviation of the same market-adjusted daily return of j over sessions t-68..t-6 (63 sessions, skipping the 5 sessions just before the release); z = e / sigma. Require at least 50 valid sessions in the window, otherwise no event. (3) Abnormal volume: AV = ln(dollar_volume[t,j]) - ln(mean dollar_volume[j] over t-68..t-6), same validity rule. (4) Matching bins: the reference pool is all event candidates of LIQ-500 members in sessions t-252..t-1 (strictly before t). Cut |z| of the pool into terciles; the candidate's bin is (sign of z, |z| tercile of the pool cutpoints), 6 bins. Within its bin, compare the candidate's AV with the AV of pool candidates in the same bin: AV at or above the (1 - leg_quantile) quantile -> side +1 (long); AV at or below the leg_quantile quantile -> side -1 (short); otherwise no event. A bin with fewer than 30 pool candidates gives no event. Before the pool covers 252 sessions of 8-K data, no events. (5) Positions: each event opens at the open of t+1 with a fixed slot of side x 1/30 of equity and is held for hold_days sessions (closed at the open after the close of t+hold_days). Slots are not resized while held. If opening the day's new slots would push gross (events plus hedge) above 1, the new slots of that day are scaled down equally to fit. title: Treasury-yield shock overshoot in equity sectors - after a large 10y yield move, long the 2 sector ETFs it pushed down, short the 2 it pushed up, hold 5 days

the liquidity providers are sector-rotation and value investors who need a few days to step in.","why":"On a day when the 10-year Treasury yield jumps or drops, rate-sensitive equity sectors are traded as a block by investors who hold them as bond substitutes or use them as rate hedges: income and dividend funds and their retail holders (utilities, REITs, staples), balanced and risk-parity books that treat them as duration, equity long/short funds that hedge rate exposure with sector ETFs, and the ETF creation/redemption that pushes those flows into the constituent stocks. On the other side financials and cyclicals are bought or sold as the 'rates-up' trade. This demand is for immediacy and is about the discount-rate move of the day, not about the sectors' cash flows, so the relative price of the rate-exposed sectors moves further than their change in value justifies. Sector rotators and value investors absorb the flow at a concession, and the rate-driven relative move partly reverses over the following week. The signal comes from the Treasury market (the yield change and each sector's historical sensitivity to it); the trade is in equity sector ETFs.","why_not_arbitraged":"The reversal trade carries rate-trend risk: yields can keep moving the same way for weeks, and a sector spread entered against a rate shock then loses before it reverts. Few desks run sector spreads against rate momentum, the effect per event is small next to the noise of a sector spread, and capital that could absorb it is slow. What is left is modest compensation for bearing rate-trend risk over a week."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"The 10-year Treasury yield (FRED DGS10) changed on day t by at least k_sigma = 1.5 times its trailing 63-observation standard deviation while the equal-weight return of the ten sector ETFs on t stayed within 2 trailing standard deviations; the event is dated at the first session d at whose close the yield of t is available (next_morning clock). Marked: the two sector ETFs with the most negative rate-explained relative move beta_i * dy(t) (trailing 252-session slope of the ETF's return minus the equal-weight return on dy) with side +1, and the two with the most positive with side -1; the other sector ETFs are the unmarked peers.","horizons":[1,3,5,10],"primary_horizon_days":5},"notes":"Brief fit: horizon 5 sessions (within 1-5); cross-asset in the strict sense: the signal is the Treasury market (FRED DGS10 and each sector's sensitivity to it), the trade is equity sector ETFs. The FRED yield is used instead of a Treasury ETF on purpose: a Treasury ETF would have to sit in the universe and would then be an unmarked peer in the event study (K-0086), contaminating the abnormal return with its own post-shock drift. Cost of that choice: the yield is usable one session late (next_morning), so entry is at the open of t+2 and the first post-shock session is missed; the lab's cross-asset reversals built over about five sessions (H-0046, H-0047), so the 5-session window should still hold most of an overshoot if it exists. How this differs from dead or related cards: (1) Not a stress rebound (K-0084, H-0041, H-0070, studies 6-7): equity-stress days (|EW move| >= 2 sigma) are excluded, so the event is a rate shock on an otherwise normal equity day, and both directions of the yield shock are marked, so generic equity drift cancels in the placebo. (2) Not H-0047 (macro-release reaction across 19 asset-class ETFs, sorted on their own reaction): events here are defined by the cause (the yield move) on any day, sorted by ex-ante rate sensitivity, inside one asset class (equity sectors), where the market-direction confound of mixing asset classes is smaller. (3) Not H-0072 (continuation in Treasury ETFs): the Treasury instrument is never traded. (4) Not the mrel linear lead-lag scan: the claim is a conditional cross-sectional reversal of the rate-explained sector move over a week, entered two sessions after the shock, not a next-day return regression. Family is short-term-reversal (liquidity provision after a flow-driven move), as H-0041 and H-0070 were filed, so the trial count is honest. Competing hypothesis, stated in advance: reaching-for-income flows (Daniel, Garlappi and Xiao, Monetary policy and reaching for income, Journal of Finance) predict that income-fund flows follow rate moves with a lag, which would make rate-driven sector moves CONTINUE; a wrong-signed result is therefore informative, not just a miss. No references are listed because no paper documents this exact reversal; the cited paper predicts the opposite sign. Expected counts: about 9-11 % of sessions have |dy| >= 1.5 sigma and most of them pass the equity filter, so roughly 400-500 event dates in 2000-2020 and 1600-2000 marked events (4 per date, 6 unmarked peers once IYR is in, 5 before); first events about 2000-01 after the 252-session beta warm-up from the card start (K-0075). Expected mean exposure about 35-40 % (gross 1 while invested, 5-session holds, replacement on new events). Typical marked sets: utilities, REITs and staples on the pushed-down side after yields rise, financials and cyclicals on the other; the sort is estimated point-in-time, not hand-picked. Beta confound (K-0074): rate-sensitive sectors are also low-market-beta sectors; marking both shock directions makes this cancel on average but adds noise. Expected size, honestly: a 1.5-sigma yield day moves the 2-vs-2 spread by very roughly 1 %; a reversal of a quarter of that gives about 0.1-0.15 % per marked ETF against peers over 5 sessions, a few times the round trip of these liquid ETFs (sector SPDRs are among the most liquid ETFs), and the placebo cloud for ~450 dates should be narrow enough (bar of order 0.1 %) to see an effect of that size. The most likely death is the strategy, not the mechanism: at that size a part-time dollar-neutral book has a Sharpe of order 0.2-0.4, below the 0.5 floor against T-bills (K-0027); it passes only if the effect is two to three times larger. ETFs have no forward data, so G4 is the ceiling.","signal":{"description":"Inputs: daily close-to-close total returns of the ten sector ETFs of the universe (from ret_co and ret_oc of sharadar_sfp) and the FRED 10-year constant-maturity Treasury yield DGS10 (fred_macro, percent, clock next_morning). Definitions: dy(t) = DGS10(t) - DGS10 of the previous valid observation, in percentage points, dated on its observation day t (days where FRED has no value give no dy). sigma_y(t) = standard deviation of the 63 valid dy observations before t (needs all 63). EW(s) = equal-weight mean return of the universe ETFs that have a return on session s; sigma_eq(t) = standard deviation of EW over the 63 sessions before t. For each ETF i, beta_i(t) = OLS slope of (r_i(s) - EW(s)) on dy(s) over the beta_days sessions s ending at t-1 on which both exist (at least 80 % of beta_days observations, otherwise i is not rankable). Event: dy(t) is at least k_sigma * sigma_y(t) in absolute value AND |EW(t)| is below 2 * sigma_eq(t) (rate shock on a day without an equity stress move). The event is acted on at the first session d at whose close dy(t) is available under the dataset clock (next_morning: normally d = the session after t). At d, compute for every rankable ETF the rate-explained relative move p_i = beta_i(t) * dy(t). The two ETFs with the lowest p_i (pushed down by the rate move) get weight +0.25 each, the two with the highest p_i (pushed up) get weight -0.25 each; all others 0 (gross 1, dollar-neutral). If a new event becomes known while a position is held, the new event's weights replace the old ones and the 5-session clock restarts. Otherwise the book is flat (cash). Missing data: an ETF with no return on t or not tradable on d is not rankable and gets no weight; if fewer than 6 ETFs are rankable at d, no event is taken. Korean retail pays the premium itself, but the strategy earns the offshore catch-up, not the premium.","why":"Korean crypto exchanges are a segmented market: foreigners cannot open accounts, residents need real-name bank accounts and face foreign-exchange limits, so KRW cannot be moved freely in and out. Makarov and Schoar (JFE 2020) document that this lets Korean prices sit well above offshore prices for long periods (the 'kimchi premium'). When Korean retail demand concentrates on particular coins, the Upbit KRW price of those coins runs ahead of their offshore price. The only way the excess demand reaches the offshore market is through capacity-limited arbitrageurs who buy the coin offshore, ship it to Korea and sell it for KRW. They then hold KRW that is hard to bring back out, so each arbitrageur can only repeat the trade slowly. That offshore buying is spread over days, so a coin whose Korean price is abnormally rich relative to its Binance price should outperform other coins on Binance over the next few days. Coins that are abnormally cheap in Korea get offshore selling (coins bought in Korea with KRW and sold offshore for USDT) and should underperform. Comparing across coins removes the KRW/USDT exchange rate and the market-wide Korean premium. What is left is coin-specific Korean demand pressure that has not yet passed through to the offshore price.","why_not_arbitraged":"The full arbitrage needs both venues, KRW banking access and repatriation of KRW, which capital controls and exchange KYC limit. I chose it because every cross-asset-class channel loadable today is already dead or crowded in this lab: daily lead-lag across stocks, ETFs, FX, macro and crypto (mrel; K-0080), stress rebounds (K-0084), macro calendars (K-0070), and rate and oil shocks (H-0056, H-0075). This card does answer K-0080's demand to say why information travels slowly through this particular channel: capital controls and KRW repatriation limits cap arbitrage capacity. FRED KRW/USD (noon fixing, stale) is deliberately not used: the cross-sectional median removes the exchange rate and the market-wide premium exactly, at the same 00:00 UTC timestamp. New data: upbit_krw_1d is essential, because the Korean price is the signal and no catalog dataset holds it. It is free, public and has a forward source, so unlike ETF and stock cards this one could reach G5. Data risks for the Archivist and the Skeptic: (1) survivorship in the signal, since the API may not serve markets Upbit delisted (several waves of delistings), and those are the pump-prone coins; (2) ticker collisions or redenominations (same symbol, different token), handled by the |r| > 20 % exclusion; (3) withdrawal suspensions freeze the arbitrage path and create premiums that cannot transmit, which adds noise against the card. Relation to existing families: not btc-lead-altcoin-lag (no BTC trigger; same coin, two venues), and not a sort on own return, funding or volume (short-term-reversal / perp-leverage-crowding). It is related to etf-premium-arbitrage (H-0037, twin-ETF gap), because it bets on convergence of a cross-venue gap. It differs in that only the offshore leg is traded, and the claim is that the segmented venue leads because arbitrage capacity is capped by capital controls, not by AP creation and redemption. If the Chair judges it the same mechanism, merge the family; I would not object. References: Makarov and Schoar (2020, JFE, 'Trading and arbitrage in cryptocurrency markets') is cited in the mechanism text only as evidence that the segmentation and the premium exist. It does not claim the cross-sectional offshore catch-up tested here, so I did not list it under references, where it would add the 20-trial literature prior meant for published return anomalies and a publication split at the start of the dev window. The Skeptic may add it if they disagree. Expected numbers (priors, not data): about 12-25 eligible coins per day in 2020-2022 (Binance top-30 perps that also trade on Upbit KRW; BNB and others do not). Events = 2 x n_leg per date, so about 6 per date on roughly 1,000 dates, about 6,000 events, with at least 4 unmarked peers per date by the 10-coin rule. Round trip on top-30 perps is about 25-40 bps. For the book to clear Sharpe 0.5 after costs, the 3-day abnormal return per leg entry must be roughly 0.5 % or more. At 0.3 % costs (turnover about 0.4-0.6 of gross per day, lower when premiums persist) eat most of it. Both legs are mostly mid-cap alts, so the beta gap between marked coins and peers should be small (K-0074), but high-premium coins may be higher beta during manias. title: Credit-ETF liquidity overshoot vs SPY/IEF anchors - tilt a 60/40 book's IEF sleeve into a credit, EM, muni or loan ETF for 5 days after a 2-sigma residual drop
card_json:
{"asset_classes":["us_etf"],"author_agent":"scout","data_requirements":[{"dataset":"sharadar_sfp","fields":["ret_co","ret_oc","dollar_volume","tradable"],"frequency":"1d","period":["2003-01-02","2020-12-31"]}],"falsification_criteria":["Mechanism: the 5-session side-adjusted abnormal return of the events is below the 95th percentile of the time-shifted placebos, or gross per event is below the round-trip cost (G1 mechanism gate).","Mechanism: the abnormal return is negative in the latest third of dev (the decay pattern of K-0060); the card treats that as a refutation even if the pooled test passes.","Mechanism: the 10-session abnormal return is negative (the residual drop kept going: credit-specific news or persistent flow, not an overshoot).","Strategy: net Sharpe on dev below the 60/40 SPY/IEF Sharpe + 0.10, or the bootstrap bound of the Sharpe difference at or below zero.","Strategy: max drawdown above 1.5 times the 60/40 drawdown (the slots buy credit during stress; this checks the falling-knife risk).","Robustness: fewer than 75 % of the neighbors (k_sigma 1.5 / 2.5, hold_days 3 / 7 and their combinations) beat 60/40, or the book does not beat 60/40 at doubled costs, or one third of dev carries more than 60 % of the log excess return."],"family":"etf-premium-arbitrage","holding_period":{"rebalance":"event","typical_days":5},"market_exposure":"long_only","mechanism":{"counterparty":"Liquidity-demanding ETF sellers (tactical and retail investors, funds raising cash) who accept a price below the liquid-market-implied value to get out the same day, and positive-feedback ETF traders (Dannhauser and Hoseinzade) who amplify the move. The strategy is paid for providing them liquidity.","why":"ETFs on illiquid fixed-income baskets (high-yield and investment-grade corporates, EM sovereigns, municipals, leveraged loans) are liquid wrappers on assets that trade by dealer quote. Investors who need liquidity in a hurry (tactical allocators, retail, funds meeting redemptions) sell the ETF, not the bonds. The authorized participants who would close the gap are also the bond dealers. Redeeming means taking bonds onto a balance sheet that is already constrained in exactly these episodes, so arbitrage capacity falls when volatility and bond illiquidity rise (Pan and Zeng), and the ETF price is pushed below the value of the claim. The liquid markets that carry the same systematic risks, US equities (credit-risk factor) and Treasuries (rate factor), are not under that wrapper-specific pressure. A move of the credit ETF far below what the same-days SPY and IEF moves imply therefore contains a temporary non-fundamental part. It should recover over the following days as dealers redeem and as slower capital (bond funds, insurers, crossover investors) buys the discount. The signal comes from the equity and Treasury markets and the trade is in the credit-type ETF, so this is a cross-asset relative-value claim.","why_not_arbitraged":"The natural arbitrageurs (APs, dealers) are balance-sheet constrained exactly when the gap opens. Redemption delivers illiquid bonds that must be warehoused or sold into a one-sided market. Relative-value capital that could hedge with SPY/Treasuries faces basis risk (credit-specific news can keep going) and funding stress in the same episodes. Most bond holders have mandates that bar them from switching into the ETF for days."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"Credit-type ETF j (LQD, HYG, JNK, EMB, MUB or BKLN) closes session t with its 5-session total return at least k_sigma = 2 residual sigmas below what its trailing-year regression on SPY and IEF returns implies (z_j,t <= -2 as defined in the signal, fit window ending 5 sessions before t), with no event for j in the previous 5 sessions. side = +1 (j should outperform the unmarked instruments). Family and difference from earlier cards: this is the etf-premium-arbitrage mechanism (wrapper price vs value of the claim), so it carries that family's trials (H-0037, H-0043, H-0077, H-0078, H-0079). (1) H-0043 asked the same question with ICE BofA OAS as the anchor and got zero events because those series are empty in dev (K-0096). That anchor cannot be fixed, so this card replaces it with liquid, real-time anchors. This also removes the confound the H-0043 lesson named, an ETF that leads a stale evaluated index. The new main rival is genuine credit-specific news that SPY/IEF do not span, which predicts a negative sign (criterion 3). (2) H-0037 compared two wrappers of the same illiquid basket. Both carry the same discount, so the gap netted out exactly the common wrapper pressure this card targets (the lesson called it mostly noise). (3) The closed-end fund cards passed the mechanism test where no arbitrage exists. Here arbitrage exists but is constrained precisely on event days. This is the open question of whether the reversion also appears in ETFs.
Known confounds, stated in advance: (a) K-0074 beta gap. The marked credit ETFs have a higher equity beta (roughly 0.3-0.5 for HYG/JNK/EMB/BKLN, less for LQD/MUB) than the peer mean (SPY, IEF, SHY, AGG and the unmarked candidates, roughly 0.1-0.2). Events cluster in equity stress, so a generic equity rebound (K-0084) would also look positive. The 1- and 3-session horizons and the latest-third sign are the best available discriminators. (b) HYG and JNK are near-twins and will often fire on the same date, so the events are fewer independent dates than marked events. (c) The trailing-year sigma reacts slowly, so the first weeks of a stress episode can produce several events in a row (the falling-knife risk, criterion 5).
Forecast, so the Librarian can check: first signals from about 2004 (LQD, the period starts 2003-01-02 and warm-up uses the card's own period, K-0075), about 2008-2009 for HYG, JNK, EMB and MUB, about 2012 for BKLN; roughly 75 instrument-years in total. Expected 300-450 marked events on 150-250 distinct dates (4-6 per instrument-year at z <= -2 with fat tails). The 3 unmarked peers per date (K-0086) are always met because SPY, IEF and SHY exist from the start. Book: mean exposure 1.0 (always invested, so the entry and decision-date minimums count rebalances), about 15-20 slot entries per year after the 2-slot cap.
Expected gain against the required margin: if a slot earns about 0.3 % over IEF per 5-session hold, the tilt adds about 15-20 x 0.20 x 0.3 % = 0.9-1.2 %/yr gross. Slot costs are about 4 legs x 2-3 bps x 0.20 per slot, about 0.05 %/yr, so they are negligible because these ETFs trade 0.3-2 bn a day. On a 60/40 book with about 9 % vol that is +0.10 to +0.13 Sharpe before the added stress-period risk of holding credit instead of IEF. The margin is reachable only if the per-event effect is at least about 0.3 %. A real effect below that is the most likely strategy death (the H-0033 / H-0046 pattern), and the mechanism verdict is the main output. No dates, episodes or tickers were chosen from performance knowledge. The candidate list is every liquid US ETF on an OTC-traded fixed-income basket with history in dev, except twins of the same index beyond HYG/JNK.","references":[{"cite":"Pan, Zeng - ETF Arbitrage under Liquidity Mismatch (ESRB Working Paper 59)","year":2017},{"cite":"Ben-David, Franzoni, Moussawi - Do ETFs Increase Volatility? Journal of Finance","year":2018},{"cite":"Haddad, Moreira, Muir - When Selling Becomes Viral: Disruptions in Debt Markets in the COVID-19 Crisis and the Fed's Response, Review of Financial Studies","year":2021},{"cite":"Dannhauser, Hoseinzade - The Unintended Consequences of Corporate Bond ETFs: Evidence from the Taper Tantrum, Review of Financial Studies","year":2022}],"signal":{"description":"Inputs: daily total returns of all ten instruments from sharadar_sfp (close-to-close return of session s = (1 + ret_co_s) * (1 + ret_oc_s) - 1, ret_co_s being previous close to open of s and ret_oc_s open to close of s). Marked candidates (credit-type ETFs) C = {LQD, HYG, JNK, EMB, MUB, BKLN}. Anchors: SPY (equity / credit-risk factor) and IEF (rate factor). SHY and AGG are never traded by the book; they are in the universe only as unmarked peers for the event study.
Residual model, per candidate j, after the close of each session t: estimate by OLS with intercept r_j,s = a_j + b1_j * r_SPY,s + b2_j * r_IEF,s + e_j,s on the 252 sessions s = t-256 .. t-5. The window ends before the 5-session signal window, so the signal window does not enter its own fit. Require at least 200 of these 252 sessions with all three returns present, else j has no signal at t. Residual sigma_j,t = standard deviation of the fitted residuals in that window. Signal window: sessions t-4 .. t (5 sessions). S_j,t = sum over the window of (r_j,s - a_j - b1_j r_SPY,s - b2_j r_IEF,s). All three returns must be present on all 5 sessions, else no signal. z_j,t = S_j,t / (sigma_j,t * sqrt(5)).
Event: z_j,t <= -k_sigma, and j has had no event in the previous hold_days sessions (an event is counted whether or not the book takes it). A candidate that has fewer than 257 sessions of price history has no signal. Before that it is simply not eligible.
Book (long-only, always fully invested): base target weights SPY 0.60, IEF 0.40 (the benchmark mix). Up to 2 tilt slots of slot_weight = 0.20 each are taken out of IEF, so IEF is never below 0 and SPY always stays at 0.60. On decision day t, new events are sorted by z ascending (most negative first) and fill free slots. A slot holds candidate j at weight 0.20 from the open of t+1 to the open of session t+1+hold_days, then returns to IEF. Events that find no free slot are dropped from the book. An instrument already held in a slot cannot take a second slot. If j stops having a price (not tradable) during a hold, its slot goes back to IEF at the next open. Targets are constant between slot changes, and the core is rebalanced to target on slot changes and at the first session of each month. Decisions after the close of t use only data up to that close and trade at the open of t+1.","params":{"hold_days":{"grid":[3,5,7],"value":5},"k_sigma":{"grid":[1.5,2.0,2.5],"value":2.0}},"timeframes":["1d"]},"title":"Credit-ETF liquidity overshoot vs SPY/IEF anchors - tilt a 60/40 book's IEF sleeve into a credit, EM, muni or loan ETF for 5 days after a 2-sigma residual drop","universe":{"instruments":["SPY","IEF","SHY","AGG","LQD","HYG","JNK","EMB","MUB","BKLN"],"kind":"instruments"}}

title: TradFi-stress-gated liquidity provision in crypto perps - when VIX is high, buy the day's BTC-residual losers and short the winners among the top-30 Binance perps, dollar-neutral, hold 3 days

The 52-week high is printed in every quote screen and newspaper table, and traders use it as a reference point: when good news pushes a stock close to its 52-week high they are reluctant to bid it through that level (it looks 'expensive' relative to the anchor), and when bad news pushes a stock far below its high they are reluctant to sell further (it looks 'cheap' relative to the anchor). Both reactions are incomplete, so the information is impounded slowly: stocks near their high drift up over the following months and stocks far below it drift down. The distinctive claim, and what this card tests, is that nearness to the high predicts returns AMONG STOCKS WITH THE SAME PAST 12-MONTH RETURN AND THE SAME VOLATILITY, i.e. it is not ordinary momentum, not the low-volatility premium (low-vol stocks sit closer to their highs mechanically) and not a stock-identity drift.","why_not_arbitraged":"The drift is slow (months), small per month relative to single-stock idiosyncratic risk, and it is a second-order sort inside momentum buckets, so it shares momentum's crash risk in sharp rebounds; capital that would arbitrage it faces long horizons, tracking error and career risk. Portfolios are formed afresh each month, so a stock that stays in a leg is marked again at the next formation. The family is reused (52-week-high-anchoring) so the H-0011 trial counts, and the card is NOT filed as momentum: momentum is neutralized, not traded. If the Chair rules the family should carry momentum trials, so be it. Expected numbers (stated before any run, K-0069/K-0098): about 200 marked events per formation (2 legs x 0.2 x ~495 eligible stocks), about 262 formation dates in dev with the 252-session warm-up (1999-01 to 2020-10), so roughly 50 000 events on ~262 dates; unmarked peers per date about 300. Effect size: George and Hwang report a 52-week-high spread of roughly half a percent per month in all stocks 1963-2001; inside momentum x volatility cells and in large caps I expect perhaps a third to a half of that, i.e. a matched spread of about 0.5-1 % over 60 sessions and a side-adjusted per-event abnormal return of about 0.25-0.5 % (half the spread), against a LIQ-500 round trip of about 6-24 bps, so cost should not bind; the placebo bar is the binding test (K-0034, K-0076: H-0054's monthly residual-momentum near miss had a bar far above cost). Strategy arithmetic: the book is fully invested (mean exposure about 0.95-1.0), about 100 equal-weighted names spread evenly over all momentum and volatility terciles, so it is close to an equal-weight LIQ-500 book plus the near-high tilt; if the long leg earns 0.1-0.25 % per month over the universe, that is +1-3 %/y at ~18 % volatility, i.e. +0.07 to +0.17 Sharpe over the equal-weight core, about the size of the +0.10 G1 margin over SPY. So the strategy is a borderline G1 case even if the mechanism is real; monthly turnover of the near-high leg should be about 30-45 % one way (persistent ranking), costs about 0.3-0.6 %/y. Most likely deaths: (1) the mechanism test lands under the placebo bar (monthly dates, overlapping 60-session windows, wide cloud), which would say there is no anchoring drift beyond momentum and volatility in liquid US stocks; (2) the sign holds early but fades or flips in the latest third (K-0060); (3) sharp junk rallies (losers far from their highs rebounding) make one third negative. The equal-weight core vs cap-weighted SPY confound (K-0064, H-0025) is real for the strategy gate; the random-entry check in G2 is the control for it. Management Science 55(1)","year":2009}],"signal":{"description":"Data: daily close-to-close total return r_t = (1+ret_co_t)(1+ret_oc_t) - 1 of each sharadar_sep stock; a total-return price index P_t = cumulative product of (1+r_t). Matching cells: split the eligible stocks into terciles of MOM and, independently, terciles of VOL (cross-sectional cut points on f), giving 9 cells. title: Cross-asset fear premium - 12 ETFs, monthly long the 3 with the richest implied-over-realized vol vs own year, short the 3 cheapest, hold 3 months

The strategy supplies risk-bearing capacity in the feared asset and withdraws it from the complacent one.","why":"Option prices carry a variance risk premium: hedgers (portfolio insurers, oil producers and consumers, gold and currency hedgers, EM allocators) buy protection, and the capital-constrained dealers and option writers who absorb that demand price the inventory risk into implied volatility (Garleanu, Pedersen, Poteshman 2009). When implied volatility is high relative to the volatility the asset is actually showing, the marginal holders of that asset's risk are unusually fearful, so the compensation they demand for holding it is high too, and the underlying earns a higher expected return over the next months (Bollerslev, Tauchen, Zhou 2009, for the S&P 500, strongest at a quarterly horizon). The signal comes from the options market and the trade is in the underlying ETFs, across asset classes. Fear episodes are often asset-specific (oil, gold and miners, China, Brazil, the euro, US small caps), so a cross-section of twelve assets with their own implied-vol indices has many more independent episodes than a single US equity timing rule (H-0055). Normalising each asset's implied/realized ratio by its own past year removes the structural level differences between assets (equity indices always carry a larger premium than gold or the euro), so the ranking rotates over time and the time-shifted placebo can test the timing, not the asset selection.","why_not_arbitraged":"It is a risk premium, not a free lunch: the long leg holds exactly the assets whose crash risk is feared most, and a crash would hit it. Dealer and cross-asset macro capital is limited and itself retreats in fear episodes. Most allocators do not combine option-implied volatility with holdings decisions across asset classes, and the premium is spread over months, which does not suit short-horizon arbitrage capital."},"mechanism_test":{"event":"At each month-end rebalance on which at least 3 x n_per_leg + 3 instruments are eligible, instrument i is in the top n_per_leg (=3) of the cross-sectional ranking of z_i,t, its implied-over-realized volatility log ratio standardized by its own previous 252 sessions (side +1: rich fear premium, should outperform the other eligible ETFs), or in the bottom n_per_leg (side -1: cheap fear premium, should underperform). Every month's leg membership is an event (each is a fresh forecast); the remaining eligible instruments are the unmarked peers (at least three on every event date by construction). Exact signal as in signal.description.","horizons":[5,10,21,42,60],"primary_horizon_days":60},"notes":"Brief fit: horizon medium (cohorts held three months, primary horizon 60 sessions), cross-asset (signal from the options market via FRED/CBOE implied-vol indices, trades in the underlying ETFs of five asset classes: US equity, EM equity, energy, precious metals and miners, the euro). Long/short across classes with gross <= 1, a gap listed in prior_studies. Relation to earlier work and honest family: H-0055 (VRP tilt of SPY against IEF) is the same mechanism and ended as a near miss with the right sign in every third, gross well above cost, but too few independent episodes; its lesson says more equity-bond pairs add events but not episodes and that implied variance measured directly was the missing input. This card measures implied vol directly per asset and uses asset-specific fear episodes for breadth; it is filed under variance-risk-premium-timing so the trials count together. It is not a short-VIXY carry rule (K-0088): nothing here holds a volatility product, and the relative design nets the common component. It does not use VIX level, realized-vol-only or calendar rules (H-0055 avoid list). Why the new dataset is essential: four of the twelve indices are already in fred_macro; with four assets the cross-section cannot leave three unmarked peers per date (K-0086), so the eight other CBOE ETF indices are needed. They come from the same FRED route as fred_vxv_1d, which the Archivist ingested before. Effective sample: the six 2011-03 series need 252 + rv_days sessions before their first z, and a cohort needs at least 9 eligible instruments, so trading and events start about 2012-04. Dev therefore holds about 104 monthly decisions; events about 104 x 6 = 620 on about 104 dates (above the 200 / 30 minimum); peers 6 per date.
